text.en: Cleopatra (born 69 BC) lived closer in time to the Moon landing (about 2,040 years) than to the building of the Great Pyramid (about 2,490 years).
About 1,710 years passed between Hammurabi's laws and Caesar's assassination — nearly as long as separates us from the Edict of Milan of 313.
Fifteen years after the Battle of Kadesh, Egypt and the Hittites signed one of the oldest known peace treaties. A copy hangs at UN headquarters.
The thylacine vanished from mainland Australia about 3,200 years ago, yet survived in Tasmania into the 20th century: the last one died in Hobart Zoo in 1936.
Cyrillic is a distant descendant of the Phoenician alphabet: Phoenician gave rise to Greek, and Greek to the letters created almost 2,000 years later.
The colossal Taupō eruption of around 232 struck a New Zealand with no people at all: Polynesians would arrive more than a thousand years later.
The Eastern Roman Empire outlived the Western one by almost 1,000 years: Rome fell in 476, Constantinople only in 1453.
China had paper by the early 2nd century, but according to tradition it reached the Islamic world only after the Battle of Talas in 751, via Chinese captives.
Kyoto (Heian-kyō) was Japan's capital for more than 1,000 years — from 794 until the emperor moved to Tokyo after the Meiji Restoration.
The oldest dated printed book, China's Diamond Sutra of 868, is almost 600 years older than the Gutenberg Bible.
Thirty-three years after the Christianization of Rus', Vikings were cutting wood in Newfoundland — tree rings date it precisely to 1021.
The same Halley's Comet embroidered on the Bayeux Tapestry in 1066 returned in 1910 — when the Earth even passed through its tail.
Oxford University is older than the Aztec state: teaching at Oxford existed by about 1096, while Tenochtitlan was founded only in 1325.
The Ottoman state, founded around 1299, still existed when the Wright brothers made the first airplane flight: the sultanate was abolished only in 1922.
Darwin and Lincoln were born on the same day: 12 February 1809.
Just 58 years separate the Wright brothers' first flight from Gagarin's, and 66 from the Moon landing — some who saw the first airplanes lived to see the Moon.
The last wild European bison was killed in the Caucasus in 1927. In 1952 bison were released into the wild again at Białowieża, descended from about a dozen zoo animals.
In autumn 1582 Catholic Europe jumped from 4 to 15 October, while Yermak’s Cossacks were marching on the capital of the Khanate of Sibir. Russia adopted the new calendar only in 1918.
The Kremlin's present walls were built by Italian masters (1485–1495). Thirteen years after they were finished, Michelangelo began the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
Ivan Fyodorov's Apostol (1564), the first precisely dated Russian printed book, came out more than a century after Gutenberg's press.
In the year St Petersburg was founded (1703), Newton became President of the Royal Society. He outlived Peter the Great by two years.
In 1868 Japan was still ruled by a shogun and samurai carried swords. Less than a century later Tokyo hosted the Olympics and launched the world's first high-speed train.
Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, the world's oldest operating place of learning, was founded by a woman, Fatima al-Fihri, 237 years before teaching began at Oxford.
Darwin spent five weeks on the Galápagos in 1835, but did not publish On the Origin of Species until 24 years later.
Women in New Zealand have voted in parliamentary elections since 1893, a quarter of a century before those in Britain, Germany or Russia.

The oldest known depiction of the night sky was recovered in a police sting in Basel. Looters with a metal detector dug up the 3,600-year-old Nebra sky disc in 1999 and sold it; in 2002 it was seized from black-market dealers.
Merit-Ptah, 'the first woman doctor in history', most likely never existed. She arose from a mix-up of two Egyptian women in a 1937 book — yet a crater on Venus has been named after her.

Ramesses II's mummy was never issued a passport — that's a myth. Flown to Paris for conservation in 1976, it was met with full military honours; the story probably grew from 'passeport', the word for its stack of paperwork.
Tutankhamun's dagger was forged from a meteorite. Its blade holds 11% nickel plus some cobalt, like iron meteorites, while iron smelted from earthly ores before the 19th century never tops 4% nickel.
Tutankhamun's trumpets were silent for over 3,000 years, then played live on BBC radio in 1939 to some 150 million listeners. According to the presenter, the silver one shattered during rehearsal.

China's oldest writing was ground up and swallowed as medicine. Villagers sold Shang oracle bones to pharmacists as 'dragon bones'; only in 1899 did the scholar Wang Yirong recognise the marks as ancient characters.
Lascaux was found thanks to a dog. In 1940, 18-year-old Marcel Ravidat noticed his dog poking into a hole left by an uprooted tree; inside were paintings 17,000 to 22,000 years old.

Altamira's paintings were found thanks to an eight-year-old girl — and her father was accused of forgery. In 1879 María led him into the cave, where he saw bison on the ceiling; experts scoffed that cavemen could not paint so well.

Neanderthals died out, yet part of them lives on in us. Their genome, decoded in 2010, showed that people of non-African descent carry a small share of Neanderthal DNA, a trace of ancient interbreeding.

One of the oldest modern human genomes came from a bone spotted by a sculptor. In 2008 mammoth-ivory carver Nikolai Peristov noticed a thighbone on the bank of the Irtysh; it proved to be 45,000 years old.

Houses built of mammoth bones were found by a farmer enlarging his cellar. In 1965 he dug up a mammoth jaw at Mezhyrich, Ukraine; archaeologists then uncovered four huts of 149 mammoth bones, about 15,000 years old.
The world's oldest statue spent 30 years in a museum as a heap of fragments. The ivory Lion-man was found in 1939 but assembled from over 200 pieces only decades later. It is 35,000–41,000 years old.

A village older than the pyramids was uncovered by a storm. In the winter of 1850 a gale stripped the sand from a dune on Orkney, revealing houses from 3180–2500 BC with stone beds, hearths and dressers facing the door.
Stonehenge was once sold at auction, for £6,600. In 1915 local barrister Cecil Chubb bought it on a whim so the stones wouldn't go to someone overseas, and in 1918 he gave it to the nation.

One of the richest Bronze Age shipwrecks was found by a sponge diver who sketched 'metal biscuits with ears'. They were copper ingots: ten tonnes of them on a 14th-century BC ship off Turkey, plus a gold scarab of Nefertiti.

A board game invented in Mesopotamia 4,500 years ago was still played in the mid-20th century. Forgotten everywhere else, it survived among the Jews of Kochi, India, until they left for Israel in the 1950s.
The Olmecs moved stone heads weighing tens of tonnes more than 150 km, and nobody knows quite how. These basalt portraits of rulers, up to 3.4 m tall, wear helmets, perhaps for war or the ballgame.

Babylonians tabulated 'Pythagorean triples' more than a thousand years before Pythagoras. The clay tablet Plimpton 322, from around 1800 BC, lists whole-number triples matching the sides of right triangles.

The oldest horse-training manual sets out a 214-day programme. Kikkuli of Mitanni wrote it around 1400 BC for Hittite chariot horses; in the 1990s an Australian researcher repeated it with Arabian horses.

The oldest Greek writing was cracked by an architect and self-taught linguist. In 1952 Michael Ventris showed that the Linear B tablets of Crete and Greece were in Greek, centuries older than the Greek alphabet.

Malta's underground temple was found by builders, who at first tried to hide it. In 1902 workers cutting cisterns for new houses broke through the roof of the Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum, later found to hold the remains of some 7,000 people.
Japan's Jōmon period lasted some 14,000 years. The gap between the earliest Jōmon pottery and the Middle Jōmon is about twice as long as the time from the Great Pyramid to today.

The legend of Atlantis may have grown out of the eruption of Santorini. So believed Spyridon Marinatos, who excavated the ash-buried Minoan town of Akrotiri: he thought Plato's tale echoed that catastrophe.

The word 'gorilla' was coined not by zoologists but by Carthaginian sailors 2,500 years ago. Hanno described hairy wild people on an African island whom his interpreters called 'gorillai'. In 1847 the name went to the ape.

A canal linked the Nile to the Red Sea some 2,400 years before Suez. Persia's Darius I completed it, and with interruptions it was used until AD 767. The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, took a different route.

Herodotus says nothing about a run from Marathon to Athens. His runner Pheidippides runs from Athens to Sparta for help, about 240 km in two days. The messenger dying with the word 'Victory!' came later and is likely a romantic invention.
The idea that the Earth goes around the Sun was proposed 1,800 years before Copernicus. Around 270 BC Aristarchus of Samos put the Sun at the centre, but his view lost out to Aristotle and Ptolemy.

The British Museum's most visited object is a piece of bureaucracy: the Rosetta Stone bears a priestly decree honouring Ptolemy V, repeated in three scripts, and has been on display almost continuously since 1802.

Cincinnati, Ohio, is named after a Roman who lived about 2,200 years before it was founded. Cincinnatus, who left power to go back to his farm, became Americans' model for Washington, and Revolutionary officers formed the Society of the Cincinnati.
In 248 Rome celebrated its 1,000th birthday. Emperor Philip the Arab held Secular Games for the millennium, counted from Romulus's founding in 753 BC. The Western Empire would fall 228 years later.
Caesar almost certainly never said 'Et tu, Brute?': Shakespeare gave him the line. Suetonius says the dictator died in silence, though some reported his last words in Greek: 'You too, child?'

The only library from antiquity to survive whole was saved by Vesuvius. The Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum kept over 1,800 scrolls, charred but intact. Found in 1752, they are still being deciphered.

Pompeii was first struck in 1592, and tunnelled straight through. Architect Domenico Fontana, digging an underground aqueduct, ran into walls with paintings and inscriptions but carried on. Excavation began only in 1748.
Sudan has twice as many pyramids as Egypt. The kings and nobles of Kush built about 255 of them, a tradition that lasted almost a thousand years, from about 700 BC to AD 350.
The name Candace was once a title of Nubian queens. Kandake meant a queen or queen mother of Kush; Greeks and Romans mistook it for a name, and through the Acts of the Apostles it became one.
'Olmec' means 'rubber people', a name given by the Aztecs. On the Gulf coast, rubber balls for the ritual ballgame were made as early as 1600 BC. What the Olmecs called themselves is unknown.

Nobody knows the real name of Teotihuacan, the largest city of the ancient Americas. 'Place where the gods were born' is the Aztec name, given centuries after its fall; the Maya called it Puh, 'Place of Reeds'.

Mesoamericans were writing zero more than 1,200 years before Fibonacci introduced it to Europe. The Long Count calendar needed a zero sign, and its earliest known date is 36 BC; Fibonacci's Liber Abaci appeared in 1202.

By the 19th century Ashoka, one of India's greatest rulers, was almost forgotten: nobody could read his edicts. The ancient Brahmi script was deciphered only in the 1830s, by James Prinsep, an assay master at a British mint.

In 1969 Erich von Däniken cited Delhi's rustless iron pillar as evidence of alien visitors. The answer is earthly: the ancient iron is rich in phosphorus, which grew a thin protective film of iron phosphate.

Every 11 February Japan marks the accession of an emperor most scholars think never existed. National Foundation Day counts from the legendary Jimmu in 660 BC; when created in 1873, it marked the 2,532nd anniversary.

The fraction 355/113 gives pi correct to six decimal places, and China had it 1,100 years before Europe. Zu Chongzhi found it in the 5th century; in Europe the Dutchman Adriaan Anthonisz arrived at it only in 1585.

Japan's Kongō Gumi stayed independent for 1,428 years, from 578 to 2006. A carpenter brought from Korea to build a temple founded it, and 40 generations of his descendants built and repaired temples until another company bought it.
'Cipher' and 'zero' are the same Arabic word. Sifr, 'empty', translated the Indian shunya, zero; it gave Latin cifra and Fibonacci's zephyrum, which became zero.
Æthelred the Unready's nickname is a pun. His name meant 'noble counsel'; Old English unræd meant 'ill counsel'. Only later, as the word fell out of use, did 'unræd' turn into 'unready'.

The real Macbeth ruled Scotland for 17 years, secure enough to go on pilgrimage to Rome in 1050, where he scattered money to the poor 'like seed'. Shakespeare made him a villain five and a half centuries later.

Two medieval would-be aviators blamed their crashes on the same thing: forgetting a tail. The story is told both of Abbas ibn Firnas in 9th-century Córdoba and of the English monk Eilmer, who leapt from a tower around 1010.
The poet Omar Khayyam helped design a calendar more accurate than the Gregorian. The Jalali calendar of 1079 drifts a day in about 5,000 years; the Gregorian (1582) every 3,330.
Movable type was invented 400 years before Gutenberg — in clay. In the 1040s the Chinese commoner Bi Sheng cut characters into sticky clay and baked them hard, as the scholar Shen Kuo recorded.
The 'Palenque astronaut' is a dead Maya king. In 1968 Erich von Däniken likened Pakal on his sarcophagus lid to a rocket pilot; the carving actually shows his descent into the underworld.
Vikings did not wear horned helmets. Texts of the period never mention them; the image was born in the 19th century, popularised above all by stagings of Wagner's operas such as the Ring (1876).

The marble lion outside Venice's Arsenal is covered in Viking runes. Swedes carved them in the 11th century, when it stood in Piraeus, Athens' port; Francesco Morosini carried it off to Venice as loot in 1687.
'Good King Wenceslas' of the English carol was never a king. St Wenceslaus, killed in 935, was Duke of Bohemia; the royal title was given posthumously, and the carol was published in 1853.
The medieval Ghana Empire was not in Ghana at all but in today's Mauritania and Mali. The British Gold Coast borrowed its name on independence in 1957.
In the 12th century Cahokia on the Mississippi was as populous as London or Paris of the day. It remained the largest city in what is now the US until the 1780s, when Philadelphia passed 40,000.
Marco Polo marvelled that in Kublai Khan's empire people paid with paper. Europe got its first banknotes only in 1661, in Sweden — 390 years after his journey began.
Marco Polo never mentions the Great Wall, but that does not prove he lied. The famous brick wall was built under the Ming, after 1368; in his day there were mostly earthen ramparts.
The Great Wall of postcards is younger than it looks: most of its brick sections were built under the Ming, after 1368. The wall of the 3rd century BC survives mostly as earthen ramparts.
Xanadu was real: Kublai Khan's summer capital, Shangdu. Marco Polo described its splendid palace, and in 1797 Coleridge's poem "Kubla Khan" turned Xanadu into a byword for fabulous luxury.
The word kamikaze is over 660 years older than Japan's suicide pilots. "Divine wind" was the name given to the typhoons that scattered Kublai Khan's fleets off Japan in 1274 and 1281.

The Mongols were stopped at Ain Jalut by former slaves. The Mamluks, warriors bought as boys and raised in barracks, ruled Egypt for 267 years, from 1250 to 1517, with sultans drawn from their own ranks.
The oldest surviving gun is Chinese, made no later than 1288, and weighs 3.5 kg. Europe's first picture of a cannon appears only in Walter de Milemete's English manuscript of 1326.

The Vietnamese twice destroyed an enemy with the same trick on the same river. In 938 and again in 1288 stakes were driven into the bed of the Bạch Đằng, and at low tide enemy ships were impaled on them.

The beaked plague doctor is not from the Black Death. The costume is first described in the 17th century and credited to the French physician Charles de Lorme in 1619, almost three centuries after the epidemic.
"Ring a Ring o' Roses" is not about the plague. The rhyme was first printed in 1881, and the plague reading only appeared in the 20th century; folklorists reject it.

English kings also styled themselves kings of France until 1801. Edward III took the title in 1340, early in the Hundred Years' War, and it was kept for 461 years, though England lost almost all its French lands in 1453.
An alliance made in the 14th century was invoked in the Second World War. In 1943 Portugal, citing its treaties with England of 1373 and 1386, let the British use bases in the Azores.
Joan of Arc was burned as a heretic in 1431, and in 1920 the Catholic Church made her a saint, 489 years later. Her conviction had already been overturned in 1456, 25 years after her death.

Eyeglasses are over 700 years old, and we know it from a sermon. In 1306 the friar Giordano da Pisa told Florentines that the art of making spectacles was "not yet twenty years" old — so they were invented around 1286.
The bronze horses of St Mark's in Venice are crusader loot. They were taken from Constantinople in 1204; in 1797 Napoleon carried them off to Paris, and in 1815 they came back.

Less than 4% survives of the world's largest encyclopedia before Wikipedia. The Yongle Encyclopedia, the work of 2,169 scholars, existed only in manuscript copies; nearly all were lost, many in a Beijing fire in 1900.
For almost 500 years the Forbidden City was home to 24 emperors. Completed in 1420, it housed 14 Ming and 10 Qing rulers until the last emperor abdicated in 1912.
The Golden Pavilion that tourists see in Kyoto is younger than the Eiffel Tower. The 1397 original was burned by a monk in 1950, and today's building dates from 1955, 66 years after the tower.
Korea's rain gauges are 198 years older than Europe's. King Sejong set up a network of identical gauges in 1441, while Europe's first was made by Benedetto Castelli only in 1639.
Tamerlane's tomb was opened on 20 June 1941, two days before Germany invaded the USSR. Legend said it bore a curse: whoever disturbed his remains would unleash war. He was reburied in 1942.
"Tamerlane" means "Timur the Lame", and his skeleton confirmed it. In 1941 anthropologist Mikhail Gerasimov found injuries to the right leg and arm and reconstructed Timur's face from his skull.
The name Dracula meant "son of the Dragon". Vlad III's father joined the Order of the Dragon in 1431 and was called Dracul, and in 1897 Bram Stoker gave the name to his vampire.

Those who fought the Wars of the Roses never called them that. The white rose of York was a real badge, but the red rose of Lancaster was rarely used; the name caught on after a Walter Scott novel of 1829.
The last English king to die in battle was found under a car park. Richard III fell at Bosworth in 1485, and in 2012 archaeologists found his remains in Leicester on the site of a vanished friary.

The first autobiography in English was dictated by a woman who could not write. The Book of Margery Kempe (c. 1438) tells of the pilgrimages of a mother of 14; its manuscript was found in a private library only in 1934.
Among the Aztecs money grew on trees: people paid in cacao beans. According to a document of 1545, a turkey cost 100 beans and a freshly picked avocado cost 3.
The Inca Empire, the largest in pre-Columbian America, lasted less than a century. Pachacuti began his conquests in 1438, and in 1533 the Spanish executed Atahualpa, just 95 years later.
The Spanish never found Machu Picchu. The Incas built it around 1450 and left within a century, and it won world fame only in 1911, when Hiram Bingham was guided there.

Colonial Rhodesia refused for decades to admit that Great Zimbabwe was built by Africans. As early as 1905 the archaeologist Randall-MacIver showed it was of local origin, yet the government pressured scholars into the 1970s.
Coins of the Kilwa Sultanate in East Africa were found in Australia. In 1944 a soldier picked up Kilwa copper coins on a beach on Marchinbar Island; how they got there is a mystery.

On finding a bronze head at Ife in 1910, the German ethnologist Leo Frobenius decided it was a relic of Atlantis. He doubted Africans could have cast it, but the Ife heads are the work of Yoruba artists.
The moai of Easter Island may have "walked". Island tradition says the statues walked on their own, and in 2012 researchers showed how: 18 people with ropes rocked an upright 5-tonne replica forward.

The word "tulip" comes from "turban". The flower reached Europe from the Ottoman Empire, its name from a Persian word for turban — and the Ottomans had their own Tulip Period some 80 years after the Dutch mania.
The Swedish warship Vasa sank in 1628 about 1,300 metres into her maiden voyage. She was raised from the harbour floor 333 years later, in 1961, almost intact.
The Dutch landed in Australia 164 years before Cook. Willem Janszoon reached Cape York Peninsula in 1606; Cook reached the east coast only in 1770.
Edo, the future Tokyo, had over a million people by the 1720s, one of the largest cities in the world. In 1590 it had been a modest castle town.
Louis XIV and the Chinese emperor Kangxi reigned side by side for over half a century, from 1661 to 1715. Louis ruled 72 years and outlived his son and grandson: his great-grandson inherited.
Janissary officers had kitchen titles: a company commander was the çorbacı, the "soup server". The cauldron was sacred to the corps, and overturning it signalled revolt.
The Catholic Church admitted its error in the Galileo case 359 years later. He was condemned in 1633; Pope John Paul II expressed regret in 1992.

Chopin's heart lies apart from his body, in Warsaw, in a jar of alcohol, probably cognac. Terrified of being buried alive, he asked his sister to take it home; she smuggled it under her clothes. It rests in a pillar of Holy Cross Church.
America's national Thanksgiving was won by the author of 'Mary Had a Little Lamb'. Sarah Josepha Hale campaigned for 17 years, and in 1863 her letter persuaded Lincoln.
Bits of the Wright Flyer have been to the Moon and Mars. Neil Armstrong carried wing fabric and propeller wood on Apollo 11, and a scrap of wing fabric flew on the Mars helicopter Ingenuity.
Einstein's Nobel Prize was not for relativity. The 1921 prize honoured 'his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect', from one of his miracle-year papers.
From 1912 to 1948 Olympic medals were awarded for poems, music and paintings. The first literature gold went to Pierre de Coubertin himself, under a pen name, and is still credited to Germany.
Gandhi spent 21 years in South Africa, from 1893 to 1914. He arrived as a young lawyer on a commercial case, and it was there that he first used nonviolent resistance.
Kimberley's Big Hole is held to be the deepest hole ever dug by hand: from 1871 to 1914 up to 50,000 miners with picks and shovels went 240 metres down and took out 2,720 kg of diamonds.
Cleopatra's Needle is almost 1,400 years older than Cleopatra: it was raised under Thutmose III around 1450 BC, and she was born in 69 BC.
Galileo saw Neptune 234 years before its discovery and took it for a star. He sketched it in December 1612 and January 1613; it was recognised as a planet only in 1846.
Stewardess Violet Jessop was aboard all three sister liners in their hour of disaster: Olympic's collision in 1911, Titanic's sinking in 1912 and Britannic's in 1916. They called her Miss Unsinkable.

The last veteran of World War I died in 2012, the year the Higgs boson was found. Florence Green, who had served in Britain's Women's Royal Air Force, died on 4 February 2012, 15 days short of her 111th birthday.

Even after confessing, one of the Cottingley cousins would not fully back down. In the early 1980s they admitted the fairies were cardboard, but Frances insisted to the end that the fifth and last photo was genuine.

Pluto was named by an 11-year-old Oxford schoolgirl. In 1930 Venetia Burney suggested the name of the god of the underworld to her grandfather, who passed it on to astronomers. She lived to see Pluto lose planet status in 2006.
Monopoly grew out of a game against monopolies. In 1904 Elizabeth Magie patented The Landlord's Game to show the evils of land grabbing; in 1935 it became the basis for Monopoly.
The Empire State Building went up in 13.5 months; the Sydney Opera House opened 16 years after its design contest. It was finished ten years late and 1,357% over budget in real terms.

Superglue was discovered by accident and promptly rejected. In 1942 Harry Coover's team, looking for clear plastic for gun sights, made a substance that stuck to everything. Only in 1951 did Coover rediscover it as an adhesive.

Three of the 20th century's greatest finds were made by non-archaeologists: Lascaux by teenagers and a dog in 1940, the Dead Sea Scrolls by Bedouin shepherds in 1947, the Terracotta Army by farmers digging a well in 1974.

The insulin patent was sold for one dollar, and the polio vaccine was never patented. In 1923 insulin's discoverers sold the rights to the University of Toronto for a token sum; in 1955 Jonas Salk sought no profit, so the vaccine would spread fast.
The title of one of Africa's most translated novels comes from an Irish poet. Chinua Achebe took Things Fall Apart (1958) from a line of W. B. Yeats's 1919 poem 'The Second Coming'.
A cure for malaria was found in a 1,600-year-old recipe. Hot extracts of sweet wormwood failed, so Tu Youyou followed advice written by Ge Hong around 340: steep the herb in cold water.

The 'curse of Tutankhamun' spared the man most to blame. Howard Carter, who opened the tomb in 1922, died only in 1939, aged 64, and Lord Carnarvon's daughter, among the first inside, lived until 1980.
For half a century, shoe shops fitted shoes under X-rays. From the 1920s to the 1970s stores had X-ray machines to show how a foot sat in a shoe; around 10,000 were sold in the US alone.
Russia's shortest year lasted four months. The year 7208 'from the Creation' began as usual on 1 September, but by Peter I's decree 31 December was followed by 1 January 1700 AD.
Beards in Russia stayed taxable for 74 years. Peter I introduced the levy in 1698, and it was abolished only in 1772, under Catherine II.

Legend says Alexander I did not die in 1825 but faked his death and lived nearly 40 more years in Siberia as the hermit Feodor Kuzmich. Historians treat it as legend, though Leo Tolstoy wrote a story about it.

There are colour photographs of the Russian Empire over a century old. In 1909–1915 Sergey Prokudin-Gorsky toured the country in a darkroom railway car provided by Nicholas II, shooting everything through three colour filters.
Russia's February 1918 had no 1st to 13th. By decree, Wednesday 31 January was followed by Thursday 14 February — Russia adopting the Gregorian calendar 336 years after Catholic Europe.

The inventor of the theremin also made one of the first bugs. In 1945 Soviet schoolchildren gave the US ambassador a carved Great Seal with Leon Theremin's listening device inside — and it hung in his Moscow office for seven years.

The Tunguska 'meteorite' left no crater. Reaching the epicentre in 1927, Kulik's expedition found trees still standing but stripped of branches, and around them 2,150 km² of forest felled in a butterfly shape: the object exploded in the air.
Earth's lowest temperature was measured at a Soviet Antarctic station: −89.2 °C at Vostok on 21 July 1983. The northern Pole of Cold lies in Yakutia, where Oymyakon recorded −67.7 °C in 1933.
Tutankhamun lived almost exactly halfway between the Great Pyramid and Cleopatra: he died about 1,240 years after the pyramid was built and about 1,290 years before Cleopatra.
The Rosetta Stone is closer in time to us than to the Great Pyramid. It was carved in 196 BC, some 2,360 years after the pyramid was built and about 2,200 years before today.

The oldest known Long Count date is closer to the 2012 'end of the world' than to the calendar's own start: carved in 36 BC, it falls 3,078 years after the mythical zero date of 3114 BC and 2,047 years before 2012.
"Soldiers, forty centuries look down upon you" — Napoleon actually undersold it. In 1798 the Great Pyramid was already about 4,360 years old: nearly 44 centuries.
Egyptian hieroglyphs outlived Cleopatra by more than 400 years. The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae on 24 August 394, when the Roman Empire was already Christian.
The Americas have their own Pompeii, five centuries younger than Italy's. Vesuvius buried Pompeii in AD 79; volcanic ash buried the Maya village of Joya de Cerén in El Salvador around AD 600.
The Inca Empire and the Khanate of Kazan arose at almost the same moment, around 1438. Both lasted roughly a century: the Spanish toppled the Incas in 1532, and Ivan the Terrible took Kazan in 1552.

The most visited stretch of the Great Wall of China is younger than the walls of the Moscow Kremlin. Badaling was built under the Ming in the early 16th century; the Kremlin walls were finished in 1495.
Harvard is 67 years older than St Petersburg: the Massachusetts college was founded in 1636, and Peter the Great founded his city on the Neva in 1703.
The first Ottoman Turkish book printed in Arabic script appeared almost 280 years after Gutenberg: a dictionary published by Ibrahim Müteferrika in Istanbul in 1729.

It took 184 years to get from the first vaccination to a world without smallpox. Jenner inoculated a boy with cowpox in 1796; in 1980 the WHO declared the disease eradicated — the only human disease ever wiped out.
The fax machine is 33 years older than the telephone. Scottish clockmaker Alexander Bain patented his 'electric printing telegraph' in 1843; Bell's telephone patent came in 1876.
A woman who met Van Gogh lived into the internet age. Jeanne Calment recalled the painter visiting her uncle's shop in Arles in 1888; she died in 1997 aged 122, the longest confirmed human life.
Work on the Sagrada Família began before the Eiffel Tower. Its first stone was laid in 1882; the tower took about two years to finish in 1889, while the Barcelona church was still unfinished in 2012.

Mark Twain came in and went out with Halley's Comet. Born in 1835, two weeks after its pass by the Sun, he predicted he would leave with it — and died in April 1910, the day after its next perihelion.

The last Emperor of China lived to see Gagarin fly. Puyi took the throne in 1908 aged two, abdicated in 1912 and died in 1967 as an ordinary citizen of the People's Republic who had worked as a gardener and an editor.
A witness to Lincoln's assassination talked about it on television. Samuel Seymour was five when he sat in Ford's Theatre in 1865; in February 1956 he appeared on the TV show I've Got a Secret.
The Great Pyramid was the tallest structure on Earth for almost 3,900 years. Only around 1311 did the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England top it; the spire fell in 1548.

The break in the Olympics lasted longer than the ancient Games themselves: they ran for about 1,170 years, traditionally from 776 BC to AD 393, and the next Games came only in 1896 — 1,503 years later.

Nearly six centuries passed between the first rules for zero and their arrival in Europe. Brahmagupta set them down in India in 628; Fibonacci's Liber Abaci introduced Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe in 1202.
China had government paper money 637 years before Europe's first banknotes. The state issued jiaozi in Sichuan in 1024; in Europe, Stockholms Banco printed the first banknotes in 1661.

Wojtek, the bear veteran of Monte Cassino, ended his days at Edinburgh Zoo in 1963. Polish comrades visited and tossed him cigarettes, which he had loved since his army days — he ate them rather than smoked.

London’s 17th-century coffee houses were called “penny universities”: for a penny, the price of entry and a cup, you could listen to scholars and merchants for hours. They gave birth to both Lloyd’s and the Stock Exchange.

The legend of Kaldi the goatherd, whose goats perked up after eating coffee berries, was first written down only in 1671. Yemen’s Sufis had been drinking coffee since the 15th century to stay awake at night prayers.
For three centuries Europeans only drank chocolate. The first bar for eating was moulded in Bristol in 1847, and the Swiss Daniel Peter invented milk chocolate only in 1875.
Some 179 years passed between the first flush toilet (1596) and the patent for the S-bend that traps smells with water (1775). Alexander Cumming’s trap is still in almost every toilet today.

Britain taxed soap for nearly a century and a half. The duty began in 1712, soap boilers’ pans were locked up at night, and only in 1853 did Gladstone abolish it, to the delight of doctors campaigning for hygiene.

For over 400 years spectacles had no arms: people held them, pinched them on the nose or tied them on with ribbons. Side-pieces resting on the ears appeared only around 1727, from the London optician Edward Scarlett.
Americans once mailed their children. When parcel post began in 1913, a few parents sent toddlers to relatives at the parcel rate. The Post Office soon banned mailing people.
The US postal motto “Neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night…” is Herodotus, describing the Persian couriers of the 5th century BC. In 1914 it was carved on New York’s main post office.
Under Peter the Great bearded men carried a token stamped “Money received”, proof of paying the beard tax. Top merchants paid 100 rubles a year; peasants paid a kopeck each time they entered a town.
Canned food was invented nearly half a century before the can opener. Early tins were opened with a hammer and chisel, or a bayonet; dedicated openers arrived only in the 1850s.
The inventor of canning never knew why it worked. Appert simply heated sealed bottles; the explanation, that heat kills microbes, came from Pasteur only in the 1860s, half a century later.

Wristwatches long counted as women’s jewellery: Breguet made the first for the Queen of Naples in 1810. Men stuck to pocket watches until World War I officers found them awkward to pull out in the trenches.

The oldest known analogue computer is over 2,000 years old. The bronze gears of the Antikythera mechanism predicted eclipses, and nothing as intricate was built again for more than a thousand years, until medieval astronomical clocks.
A steam turbine was built in Alexandria in the 1st century, about 1,700 years before Watt's engine. Hero's sphere spun on jets of steam, but no one gave it any work to do, and it stayed a curiosity.

The 'ancient battery' from Iraq most likely held scrolls. Wilhelm König proposed in 1938 that it was a galvanic cell, but no wires or devices were found with it, and similar jars were used to store papyri.

For nearly 1,400 years doctors learned human anatomy from descriptions of monkeys. In the 2nd century Galen dissected macaques and pigs, and his errors were repeated until Vesalius checked against real human bodies in 1543.

In 1804 a medical student drank yellow fever patients' vomit to prove the disease was not contagious. Stubbins Ffirth never got sick, but he was wrong: mosquitoes spread it, as was finally shown in Cuba in 1900.

To experiment on himself, a surgeon tricked a nurse. Gerda Ditzen agreed to be the subject, but Werner Forssmann strapped her to the table and threaded the catheter into his own heart instead. It won him a Nobel Prize 27 years later.
Phineas Gage carried around the iron rod that had gone through his head. The 6 kg bar stayed with him for the rest of his life, and now it is displayed beside his skull in a Harvard medical museum.
Since its discovery Neptune has gone round the Sun just once. It was found in 1846, and a Neptunian year lasts about 165 Earth years, so the planet celebrated its first 'birthday' in 2011.

Having found Neptune on paper, Le Verrier used the same method to predict a planet that isn't there. In 1859 he proposed Vulcan, near the Sun, to explain Mercury's orbit; people 'saw' it for decades until Einstein explained the orbit in 1915 without it.

A bulb in a Livermore fire station has been lit since 1901 and has hardly ever been off. When it was moved to a new station in 1976 it went dark for about 22 minutes; rather than unscrew it, they cut the cord.

The keeper of the pitch drop experiment waited 52 years to see a drop fall, and never did. John Mainstone once missed one by stepping out for tea, and in 2000 the camera failed in a thunderstorm. The experiment won an Ig Nobel Prize.
Galileo's middle finger is on display in a Florence museum. It was removed in 1737 when his remains were moved to a new tomb, and it now stands in a glass jar, pointing at the sky.

Galileo's falling-bodies experiment was tested on the Moon. In 1971 Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather together, and with no air they hit the dust at the same instant.

Gunpowder was invented by people looking for the elixir of life. Chinese Taoist alchemists mixing saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal in search of immortality got a mixture that flared up and burned their hands and faces.
In 1865 Jules Verne sent three men to the Moon from Florida, just as Apollo 11 did 104 years later. In the sequel his crew also came home with a splashdown in the Pacific.

Ceres was counted as a planet for half a century. Found on the first day of the 19th century, 1 January 1801, it was listed among the planets until dozens of similar bodies turned up. Now, like Pluto, it is a dwarf planet.
Uranus was almost named after an English king. William Herschel, who discovered it in 1781, proposed 'George's Star' after George III, and the name hung on in Britain for nearly 70 years.

Lost works of Archimedes turned up beneath prayers. In 1229 a monk scraped an old manuscript and wrote a prayer book over it; in 1906 scholar Heiberg spotted Archimedes underneath, and the full text was finally read using X-rays.
In ancient Egypt a pregnancy test used grain: a woman urinated on wheat and barley, and if they sprouted, she was pregnant. When scientists tried it in 1963, the method worked in about 70% of cases.

A schoolboy in Tanganyika noticed what Aristotle had written about: hot water sometimes freezes faster than cold. Erasto Mpemba saw it in 1963 while making ice cream; he was mocked, but the effect now bears his name.

The meteorologist who said continents move was mocked for half a century. Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, but was vindicated only in the 1960s with plate tectonics, three decades after he died in Greenland.

Tyre rubber was invented by dropping some on a stove. In 1839 Charles Goodyear, the story goes, accidentally heated rubber mixed with sulphur and got a tough material, yet he died in debt, and the famous tyre company was named after him by others.
Medieval scholars knew the Earth was round. Sacrobosco's textbook On the Sphere, written around 1230, was standard reading in European universities for some 400 years.
The idea that medieval people believed in a flat Earth is a 19th-century invention, popularised among others by Washington Irving's romanticised 1828 biography of Columbus.
The iron maiden is not medieval: it was dreamed up in the late 18th century. The first account appeared in 1793, and the museum examples were pieced together from unrelated old artefacts.
No one knows which gesture Roman crowds used to doom a gladiator. 'Thumbs down' comes from Gérôme's 1872 painting Pollice Verso — the Latin just means 'with a turned thumb', direction unknown.

Ivan Susanin's deed is known from one royal charter of 1619, which says nothing about swamps or leading enemies astray — only that 'Polish and Lithuanian people' tortured him. The rest came from 19th-century writers and Glinka.
The Library of Alexandria did not vanish in a single blaze. Caesar's fire of 48 BC damaged it, but it declined over centuries as funding dried up and scholars were driven out.
Claims that the Great Wall is visible from the Moon were printed in 1932, 37 years before anyone got there. Astronauts saw no such thing: the wall is too narrow, and hard to spot even from low orbit.

Chastity belts were almost certainly not worn in the Middle Ages. Nearly all museum examples were made in the 18th–19th centuries, and medieval mentions are jokes or allegories; the British Museum took its own off display.
'And yet it moves!' first appeared in print in 1757, 115 years after Galileo's death. Saying it before the Inquisition would have been suicidal, and no contemporary records it.
Einstein never failed maths: he had mastered calculus before he was 15. Shown a 1935 newspaper item claiming otherwise, he replied: 'I never failed in mathematics.'
Witch hunting was early modern, not medieval. It peaked around 1560–1630, the age of Shakespeare, Galileo and Kepler, and the Malleus Maleficarum was printed after Gutenberg.
Catherine the Great did not sell Alaska: she died 71 years before the deal. It was Alexander II who sold it to the United States in 1867, for $7.2 million.
The druids did not build Stonehenge: it went up around 3000–2000 BC, some two thousand years before druids appear in Britain. The link was invented by 17th- and 18th-century antiquarians.
Napoleon's soldiers did not shoot the nose off the Sphinx. It is already missing in Frederic Norden's drawings from 1737, and the historian al-Maqrizi wrote that a zealot defaced the statue in 1378.

The Moscow Kremlin was white for a long time. Italian builders raised its walls in red brick, but from the late 17th century they were whitewashed, and the red only reappeared by the early 20th century.
The Tsar Cannon, contrary to the saying, seems to have been fired. During its 1980 restoration Artillery Academy experts found powder residue in the barrel and concluded it had fired at least once.
The Maya calendar never predicted the end of the world in 2012. On 21 December 2012 the 13th b'ak'tun of the Long Count simply ended, much as a year ends at midnight on 31 December.
